questions.stem: A vessel is overtaking another when she comes up with her from a direction more than how far abaft her beam?
options: 10 degrees
22.5 degrees
45 degrees
67.5 degrees
questions.explanation: The overtaking sector starts 22.5 degrees abaft the beam, the same line where the sidelight arc ends. 67.5 degrees is half the sternlight arc measured from dead astern, which is the same boundary measured from the other end, not from the beam.

questions.stem: At night you are coming up on a vessel ahead. Which lights would you see if you are in her overtaking sector?
options: Her red and her green sidelights
Her sternlight only, and neither sidelight
Her masthead light and one sidelight
Her sternlight and one sidelight
questions.explanation: Rule 13 describes the overtaking position as one from which you would see only the sternlight and neither sidelight. If you can see a sidelight you are forward of the 22.5 degree line, and if you can see both sidelights you are ahead of her.

questions.stem: A sailing vessel under sail is overtaking a power-driven tug in clear weather. Which vessel keeps out of the way?
options: The tug, because power-driven vessels keep out of the way of sailing vessels
The sailing vessel, because she is overtaking
Both must alter to starboard
Neither, because Rule 13 applies only between power-driven vessels
questions.explanation: Rule 13 applies to any vessel overtaking any other vessel, notwithstanding the rest of Sections I and II. Rule 18 itself starts 'except where Rules 9, 10 and 13 otherwise require', so the usual power-gives-way-to-sail order does not help an overtaking sailboat.

questions.stem: At night you are coming up on another vessel and her light keeps flickering between her green sidelight and her white sternlight. What should you do?
options: Treat it as a crossing situation, since you can sometimes see her green light
Assume you are overtaking and keep out of the way
Assume she is overtaking you
Hold course and speed, since the situation is unclear
questions.explanation: You are right on the 22.5 degree line, so you are in doubt. Rule 13 says that when in any doubt, assume you are overtaking and act accordingly. Choosing 'crossing' could let you claim to be stand-on when you are not. Holding course and speed is not an option for a vessel that may be overtaking.

questions.stem: You are overtaking a slower vessel on her starboard side. As you draw ahead, she comes to bear on your port quarter and her bearing from you keeps changing. Which statement is correct?
options: Once she is abaft your beam you have become the stand-on vessel
It is now a crossing (Rule 15)
You stay overtaking until finally past and clear
She must now keep clear because she has you on her starboard bow
questions.explanation: Rule 13(d) says a later change of bearing does not make the overtaking vessel a crossing vessel or relieve her of the duty to keep clear until finally past and clear. Treating the new geometry as a crossing would hand the duty to the vessel you are overtaking, which the rule forbids.

questions.stem: You are steering 045 degrees true. A power-driven vessel bears 180 degrees true from you and is closing. Is she overtaking you?
options: No; she bears 45 degrees abaft your beam on the port side, so this is a crossing situation
Yes; at 135 relative she is over 22.5 deg abaft the beam
No; a vessel is only overtaking if she is dead astern
Yes, but only if she is faster than 20 knots
questions.explanation: Relative bearing = 180 - 045 = 135 degrees, which is on your starboard side, 45 degrees abaft the beam (the beam is at 090 relative). Anything more than 22.5 degrees abaft the beam (more than 112.5 relative on the starboard side) is in the overtaking sector. She is on your starboard quarter, not port, and the rule sets no speed limit or 'dead astern' test.

questions.stem: What are the arcs of visibility of a sidelight and a sternlight, and how do they relate to the overtaking rule?
options: Side 112.5, stern 135; side cut-off 22.5 abaft beam starts the sector
Sidelight 135 degrees, sternlight 112.5 degrees; the overtaking sector begins at the beam
Sidelight 90 degrees, sternlight 180 degrees; the overtaking sector begins at the beam
Sidelight 112.5 degrees, sternlight 225 degrees; the overtaking sector begins 45 degrees abaft the beam
questions.explanation: Each sidelight shows from right ahead to 22.5 degrees abaft the beam (90 + 22.5 = 112.5 degrees). The sternlight covers the remaining 135 degrees (360 - 2 x 112.5), which is 67.5 degrees each side of dead astern. 225 degrees is the masthead light arc, not the sternlight.

questions.stem: The Canadian Regulations add a paragraph (e) to Rule 13. Where does it apply?
options: In all Canadian waters, including the BC coast
Only in the waters of the Great Lakes Basin
Only in narrow channels with a tidal stream
Only to vessels under 20 metres
questions.explanation: Rule 13(e) applies in the waters of the Great Lakes Basin, where some power-driven vessels may show an all-round white light instead of a separate sternlight. It does not change the overtaking rule on the BC coast. The tidal-stream provision you may be thinking of is the Canadian addition to Rule 9.
